flawed_step: Step 2: From the fact that both algorithms output a minimum spanning tree, one cannot conclude that they output the same edge set. Equal-weight ties can produce multiple distinct minimum spanning trees.
counterexample: Let the connected graph have vertices {A,B,C} and edges AB, AC, BC, each of weight 1. Legal Kruskal run: break ties in the order AB, AC, BC. Kruskal accepts AB and AC, producing {AB,AC}. Legal Prim run: start at B; first break the tie by choosing BC, then choose BA from the two weight-1 edges crossing from {B,C} to {A}. Prim produces {BC,AB}. These edge sets differ. Each is a spanning tree with two edges and total weight 2. Every spanning tree of this graph has exactly two edges, each of weight 1, so weight 2 is minimum. Thus both outputs are minimum spanning trees.
assessment_summary: The universal claim fails because unspecified tie-breaking permits Kruskal and Prim to select different minimum spanning trees on the same graph.
